title: Θεῶν ἔρις
about: Athena, wounded on her aegis by Ares, fells him with a boundary-stone, and Aphrodite, leading him away, is struck down by Athena in her turn. Hera is pleased. Poseidon then challenges Apollo to begin the fight, recalling how the two of them once served the cheating Laomedon at Troy, but Apollo refuses to fight his father’s brother for the sake of mortals. Artemis taunts her brother, and Hera beats her about the ears with her own bow; she flees in tears. Hermes will not fight Leto, and bids her boast of her victory among the gods.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν οὔτησε κατ’ αἰγίδα θυσσανόεσσαν
σμερδαλέην, ἣν οὐδὲ Διὸς δάμνησι κεραυνός·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he thrust at the aegis, tasselled,
frightful, which not even the thunderbolt of Zeus subdues;
sentences.i: So he spoke and stabbed at the tasselled aegis, the frightful one that not even the thunderbolt of Zeus overcomes;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Ares’ speech in the last part, and he is the one who thrusts. The aegis is Athena’s, though she is not named yet. θυσσανόεσσαν ‘tasselled’ and σμερδαλέην ‘frightful’ both agree with αἰγίδα. οὔτησε is from οὐτάω, a thrust from close at hand (here it lands on the aegis and wounds no one), and δάμνησι is the present of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, an older form of δαμάζω.

sentences.t: τῇ μιν Ἄρης οὔτησε μιαιφόνος ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ.
sentences.l: There at her Ares thrust, blood-stained, with a long spear.
sentences.i: There blood-stained Ares stabbed at her with his long spear.
sentences.n: τῇ is ‘there’, on the aegis, and μιν ‘her’ is Athena; the spear lands on the aegis and does not wound her. μιαιφόνος Ἄρης is the stock ‘blood-stained Ares’, translated every time. ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ is a dative of means, ‘with a long spear’; ἔγχεϊ is the uncontracted dative of ἔγχος.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἀναχασσαμένη λίθον εἵλετο χειρὶ παχείῃ
κείμενον ἐν πεδίῳ μέλανα τρηχύν τε μέγαν τε,
τόν ῥ’ ἄνδρες πρότεροι θέσαν ἔμμεναι οὖρον ἀρούρης·
sentences.i: But she drew back and took in her stout hand a stone that lay on the plain, black and rough and great, which men of an earlier time had set there as a boundary of the plough-land;
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is Athena. ἀναχασσαμένη is the aorist middle participle of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’, and χειρὶ παχείῃ is the stock ‘stout hand’. Line 404 repeats the line that describes Hector’s stone at 7.265. τόν is a relative, ‘which’; θέσαν is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι, and οὖρον is ‘boundary-mark’ (Ionic for ὅρος), a stone set to divide fields.

sentences.t: τῷ βάλε θοῦρον Ἄρηα κατ’ αὐχένα, λῦσε δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.l: With it she hit impetuous Ares on the neck, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.i: She hit impetuous Ares on the neck with it, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.n: τῷ ‘with it’ is the stone. βάλε is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’, and θοῦρον Ἄρηα is the stock ‘impetuous Ares’. λῦσε γυῖα ‘loosed his limbs’ is the usual idiom for a blow that brings a man down; here the god is felled, not killed.

sentences.t:
ἑπτὰ δ’ ἐπέσχε πέλεθρα πεσών, ἐκόνισε δὲ χαίτας,
τεύχεά τ’ ἀμφαράβησε·
sentences.l:
And seven plethra he covered in falling, and he made his hair dusty,
and his armour clanged about him;
sentences.i: and as he fell he covered seven plethra, and soiled his hair with dust, and his armour clanged about him;
sentences.n: πέλεθρα is the plural of πέλεθρον, a measure of length, about a hundred feet, so the fallen god is huge. ἐπέσχε is the aorist of ἐπέχω, here ‘stretched over, covered’. ἐκόνισε ‘made dusty’ comes from κόνις ‘dust’, and ἀμφαράβησε ‘clanged around’ from ἀραβέω, the noise of armour. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
γέλασσε δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη,
καί οἱ ἐπευχομένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
and laughed Pallas Athena,
and over him, vaunting, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: and Pallas Athena laughed, and in triumph over him spoke winged words:
sentences.n: γέλασσε is the aorist of γελάω ‘laugh’, with doubled σ. ἐπευχομένη ‘vaunting’ is triumphant boasting over a beaten man, and οἱ ‘him’ is Ares. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock ‘winged words she spoke’.

sentences.t:
νηπύτι’ οὐδέ νύ πώ περ ἐπεφράσω ὅσσον ἀρείων
εὔχομ’ ἐγὼν ἔμεναι, ὅτι μοι μένος ἰσοφαρίζεις.
sentences.l:
“Childish one, not even yet have you taken note how much better
I declare myself to be, that to me in might you compare yourself.
sentences.i: “You child, you have not yet taken note how much better I declare myself to be than you, that you match yourself with me in might.
sentences.n: Athena’s taunt. νηπύτιε ‘childish one’ is a scolding address (it returns at 441 and 474). ἐπεφράσω is the aorist middle of ἐπιφράζομαι ‘take note of’, and πώ περ is ‘even yet’. ἀρείων is ‘better’, and εὔχομαι ‘I declare’ takes the infinitive ἔμεναι (Attic εἶναι). ἰσοφαρίζεις ‘you compare yourself’ (‘match yourself’ in the English) has μοι ‘with me’ and μένος ‘in might’ as an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
οὕτω κεν τῆς μητρὸς ἐρινύας ἐξαποτίνοις,
ἥ τοι χωομένη κακὰ μήδεται οὕνεκ’ Ἀχαιοὺς
κάλλιπες, αὐτὰρ Τρωσὶν ὑπερφιάλοισιν ἀμύνεις.
sentences.l:
Thus might you pay off in full your mother’s Erinyes,
she who indeed, incensed, devises evils, because the Achaeans
you abandoned, and the overweening Trojans you defend.”
sentences.i: So you would be paying in full for your mother’s Erinyes; she is incensed and devises evils because you abandoned the Achaeans and defend the overweening Trojans.”
sentences.n: ἐξαποτίνοις is an optative with κεν, ‘you would pay in full’. ἐρινύες are the avenging spirits that carry out a mother’s curse: Ares is repaid for Hera’s anger. ἥ is Hera, and τοι is either ‘indeed’ or ‘to you’. κάλλιπες is κατέλιπες, aorist of καταλείπω ‘abandon’. ὑπερφιάλοισιν ‘overweening’ is translated every time.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα πάλιν τρέπεν ὄσσε φαεινώ·
sentences.l: So then having spoken, back she turned her two eyes, shining;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and turned her shining eyes away;
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins, and Athena’s speech is over. τρέπεν is the unaugmented imperfect of τρέπω ‘turn’. ὄσσε ‘eyes’ and φαεινώ ‘shining’ are duals, the pair of eyes, and πάλιν is ‘back, away’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄγε χειρὸς ἑλοῦσα Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη
πυκνὰ μάλα στενάχοντα·
sentences.l:
Him led, by the hand taking him, Zeus’ daughter Aphrodite,
groaning very thickly;
sentences.i: Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, took him by the hand and led him, groaning again and again;
sentences.n: τόν is Ares. ἄγε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω ‘lead’, and χειρὸς ἑλοῦσα ‘taking him by the hand’ puts the part held in the genitive. Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη is ‘Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus’. πυκνὰ μάλα ‘very thickly’ describes the groans coming fast, and στενάχοντα agrees with τόν.

sentences.t: μόγις δ’ ἐσαγείρετο θυμόν.
sentences.l: and hardly was he gathering in his spirit.
sentences.i: and with difficulty he was drawing his spirit together.
sentences.n: ἐσαγείρετο is the imperfect middle of εἰσαγείρομαι ‘gather in’, written with ἐσ-, and without augment. μόγις is ‘with difficulty’. θυμόν is the spirit, which the verb pictures him pulling together after the blow.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
αὐτίκ’ Ἀθηναίην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And her when then noticed the goddess, white-armed Hera,
at once to Athena winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: And when the goddess, white-armed Hera, noticed her, she at once spoke winged words to Athena:
sentences.n: τὴν is Aphrodite, ‘her’, and the subject is θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη, the stock ‘the goddess, white-armed Hera’. ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε is ‘when then she noticed’. Line 419 is the stock introduction ‘winged words she spoke’, with Athena as the person addressed.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος Ἀτρυτώνη
καὶ δ’ αὖθ’ ἡ κυνάμυια ἄγει βροτολοιγὸν Ἄρηα
δηΐου ἐκ πολέμοιο κατὰ κλόνον·
sentences.i: “Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone: and see, that dog-fly is leading Ares, the ruin of mortals, out of hostile war, through the turmoil;
sentences.n: Hera speaks to Athena. ὢ πόποι is ‘Ah’; Ἀτρυτώνη is a cult-title of Athena, traditionally ‘the Unwearied’, though the formation is irregular and the sense not fully certain. ἡ κυνάμυια ‘the dog-fly’ is Aphrodite, called by the word Ares used to Athena at 394. βροτολοιγὸν Ἄρηα is the stock ‘mortal-ruining Ares’; δηΐου ‘hostile’; κλόνον ‘turmoil’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μέτελθε.
sentences.l: but go in pursuit.”
sentences.i: But go in pursuit.”
sentences.n: μέτελθε is the aorist imperative of μετέρχομαι ‘go after’. It has no object in the Greek, and Aphrodite and Ares are the ones meant. Hera’s speech ends here, and Athena acts on it in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’, Ἀθηναίη δὲ μετέσσυτο, χαῖρε δὲ θυμῷ,
καί ῥ’ ἐπιεισαμένη πρὸς στήθεα χειρὶ παχείῃ
ἤλασε·
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Athena rushed in pursuit, glad in spirit, and springing upon her struck her on the breast with her stout hand;
sentences.n: φάτ’ is the unaugmented aorist of φημί. μετέσσυτο is the aorist of μετασεύομαι ‘rush after’, with doubled σ. ἐπιεισαμένη is an aorist middle participle, ‘rushing upon’. πρὸς στήθεα is ‘at the breast’, and ἤλασε the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘strike’, with no object stated; τῆς in the next unit says who is struck.

sentences.t: τῆς δ’ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ.
sentences.l: And her knees were loosed on the spot, and her dear heart.
sentences.i: and her knees gave way at once, and her heart too.
sentences.n: τῆς ‘of her’ is Aphrodite, and λύτο is the unaugmented aorist passive of λύω ‘loosen’. αὐτοῦ is ‘on the spot’. Knees and heart failing is the usual picture of a faint or a fall; the same line stands at Odyssey 4.703.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ἄρ’ ἄμφω κεῖντο ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ,
ἣ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπευχομένη ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευε·
sentences.l:
The two, then, both lay on the much-nourishing earth,
and she, vaunting, winged words spoke:
sentences.i: Both of them lay on the earth that feeds so many, and she, in triumph over them, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: τὼ … ἄμφω ‘the two … both’ are duals, Ares and Aphrodite, with the plural verb κεῖντο (= ἔκειντο) ‘lay’. χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ is the stock ‘the much-nourishing earth’. ἣ δ’ is Athena. ἐπευχομένη ‘vaunting’ is as at 408–409.

sentences.t:
τοιοῦτοι νῦν πάντες ὅσοι Τρώεσσιν ἀρωγοὶ
εἶεν, ὅτ’ Ἀργείοισι μαχοίατο θωρηκτῇσιν,
ὧδέ τε θαρσαλέοι καὶ τλήμονες, ὡς Ἀφροδίτη
ἦλθεν Ἄρῃ ἐπίκουρος ἐμῷ μένει ἀντιόωσα·
sentences.l:
“Such now may all be, as many as are helpers to the Trojans,
when they fight with the corseleted Argives,
and thus bold and enduring, as Aphrodite
came, an ally to Ares, meeting my might;
sentences.i: “Would that all who are helpers to the Trojans were like this now, when they fight the corseleted Argives, as bold and enduring as Aphrodite was when she came as an ally to Ares, to meet my might;
sentences.n: Athena’s second speech. εἶεν is an optative of wish, ‘may they be’, with τοιοῦτοι … ὅσοι ‘such … as many as’. ἀρωγοί ‘helpers’; μαχοίατο is the optative of μάχομαι; θωρηκτῇσιν ‘corseleted’ goes with Ἀργείοισι. θαρσαλέοι ‘bold’, τλήμονες ‘enduring’. ἐπίκουρος ‘ally’; ἀντιόωσα ‘meeting’ takes the dative ἐμῷ μένει.

sentences.t:
τώ κεν δὴ πάλαι ἄμμες ἐπαυσάμεθα πτολέμοιο
Ἰλίου ἐκπέρσαντες ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον.
sentences.l:
then indeed long ago we should have ceased from war,
having sacked the well-built citadel of Ilium.”
sentences.i: then long ago we would have stopped fighting, having sacked the well-built citadel of Ilium.”
sentences.n: τώ κεν … ἐπαυσάμεθα is ‘then we would have ceased’, an unreal past condition. ἄμμες is the Aeolic ‘we’ (Attic ἡμεῖς), and πτολέμοιο is πολέμου. ἐκπέρσαντες ‘having sacked’; ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον is the stock ‘well-built citadel’. The speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and smiled the goddess, white-armed Hera.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the goddess, white-armed Hera, smiled.
sentences.n: φάτο is the unaugmented aorist of φημί, and Athena is the speaker. μείδησεν is the aorist of μειδάω ‘smile’, and θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη is the stock ‘the goddess, white-armed Hera’, translated each time.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Ἀπόλλωνα προσέφη κρείων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.l: But to Apollo addressed the lord earth-shaker:
sentences.i: And the lord earth-shaker said to Apollo:
sentences.n: κρείων ἐνοσίχθων is Poseidon, ‘the lord earth-shaker’, translated each time. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’ (the augment sits between πρός and the stem). He speaks to Apollo, and so begins the quarrel between the two gods who once built Troy’s wall.

sentences.t: Φοῖβε τί ἢ δὴ νῶϊ διέσταμεν;
sentences.l: “Phoebus, why then do we two stand apart?
sentences.i: “Phoebus, why do we two stand apart?
sentences.n: Φοῖβε is the vocative of Φοῖβος. νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’, and διέσταμεν the perfect of διίστημι, here intransitive ‘stand apart’. τί ἢ δή adds impatience, ‘why then?’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ ἔοικεν
ἀρξάντων ἑτέρων·
sentences.l:
Nor is it fitting,
others having begun;
sentences.i: It is not fitting, now that others have begun;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ ἔοικεν is ‘nor is it fitting’, with the genitive absolute ἀρξάντων ἑτέρων ‘others having begun’: the other gods are already fighting. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν αἴσχιον αἴ κ’ ἀμαχητὶ
ἴομεν Οὔλυμπον δὲ Διὸς ποτὶ χαλκοβατὲς δῶ.
sentences.l:
this is more shameful, if without a fight we go
to Olympus, to the bronze-floored house of Zeus.
sentences.i: it will be the more shameful if we go without a fight to Olympus, to the house of Zeus with the bronze floor.
sentences.n: τὸ μὲν αἴσχιον is ‘this will be the more shameful’. αἴ κ’ is εἰ κε ‘if’, and ἴομεν the subjunctive ‘we go’ (Attic ἴωμεν). ἀμαχητί is ‘without a fight’. Οὔλυμπον δέ has -δε of direction, and ποτί is πρός. χαλκοβατὲς δῶ is ‘the bronze-floored house’ (δῶ is short for δῶμα); whether the word means a bronze floor or a bronze threshold is disputed.

sentences.t: ἄρχε·
sentences.l: Begin;
sentences.i: You begin;
sentences.n: ἄρχε is the imperative of ἄρχω ‘begin’: Poseidon bids Apollo start the fight, and gives his reasons in the next two units. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: σὺ γὰρ γενεῆφι νεώτερος·
sentences.l: for you are younger in birth;
sentences.i: for you are the younger by birth;
sentences.n: γενεῆφι has the old ending -φι, here ‘by birth’. νεώτερος is the comparative ‘younger’, and γάρ gives the reason for ἄρχε. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔμοιγε
καλόν, ἐπεὶ πρότερος γενόμην καὶ πλείονα οἶδα.
sentences.l:
for not to me, at least,
is it fine, since I was born earlier and know more.
sentences.i: for it would not be fine for me, at least, since I was born earlier and know more.
sentences.n: ἔμοιγε is ‘for me at least’, and καλόν ‘fine’, in the sense of seemly, has ἐστί understood. πρότερος γενόμην is ‘I was born earlier’; πλείονα οἶδα ‘I know more’, with οἶδα the perfect used as a present. The elder should not be the one to begin.

sentences.t: νηπύτι’ ὡς ἄνοον κραδίην ἔχες·
sentences.l: Childish one, how senseless a heart you had!
sentences.i: You child, how senseless a heart you had!
sentences.n: νηπύτι’ is the elided vocative ‘childish one’. ὡς is exclamatory ‘how’, and ἄνοον ‘senseless’ is ἀ- + νόος. ἔχες is the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω (Attic εἶχες). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ νυ τῶν περ
μέμνηαι ὅσα δὴ πάθομεν κακὰ Ἴλιον ἀμφὶ
μοῦνοι νῶϊ θεῶν,
sentences.l:
and not even of those things now
do you remember, how many evils we suffered around Ilium,
we two alone of the gods,
sentences.i: and you do not even remember those things, how many evils we two alone of the gods suffered around Ilium,
sentences.n: οὐδέ … περ is ‘and not even’, with τῶν ‘those things’. μέμνηαι is the uncontracted form of μέμνῃ ‘you remember’ and takes the genitive. ὅσα … κακά is ‘how many evils’, πάθομεν the aorist of πάσχω, and Ἴλιον ἀμφί ‘around Ilium’. μοῦνοι νῶϊ θεῶν is ‘we two alone of the gods’.

sentences.t:
ὅτ’ ἀγήνορι Λαομέδοντι
πὰρ Διὸς ἐλθόντες θητεύσαμεν εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν
μισθῷ ἔπι ῥητῷ·
sentences.i: when we came from Zeus to proud Laomedon and worked for hire for a year, for an agreed wage;
sentences.n: ἀγήνωρ is ‘manly, proud’, translated each time, and Laomedon is king of Troy. πὰρ Διός is παρὰ Διός ‘from Zeus’s side’. θητεύσαμεν is the aorist of θητεύω ‘work for hire’ (θής is a hired man), and εἰς ἐνιαυτόν ‘for a year’. μισθῷ ἔπι ῥητῷ is ‘for an agreed wage’, ἔπι standing after its noun.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ σημαίνων ἐπέτελλεν.
sentences.l: and he, giving orders, laid his charges.
sentences.i: and he gave the orders and laid his charges on us.
sentences.n: ὃ is Laomedon, the king they served. σημαίνων is ‘giving orders’, and ἐπέτελλεν the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘lay a charge’. The Greek leaves the object unsaid; the two gods are meant. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ἐγὼ Τρώεσσι πόλιν πέρι τεῖχος ἔδειμα
εὐρύ τε καὶ μάλα καλόν, ἵν’ ἄρρηκτος πόλις εἴη·
sentences.l:
I, for my part, for the Trojans around the city a wall built,
both broad and very fine, that unbreakable the city might be;
sentences.i: For my part, I built the Trojans a wall around their city, broad and very fine, so that the city might be unbreakable;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ἐγώ is ‘I for my part’ (ἤτοι is printed as one word). ἔδειμα is the aorist of δέμω ‘build’, and πόλιν πέρι is ‘around the city’, πέρι after its noun. εὐρύ ‘broad’ and καλόν ‘fine’ agree with τεῖχος. ἵν’ … εἴη is a purpose clause, and ἄρρηκτος is ‘unbreakable’.

sentences.t:
Φοῖβε σὺ δ’ εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς βουκολέεσκες
Ἴδης ἐν κνημοῖσι πολυπτύχου ὑληέσσης.
sentences.l:
Phoebus, but you the rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle were wont to herd
in the spurs of Ida, many-folded, wooded.
sentences.i: while you, Phoebus, used to herd the cattle of rolling gait and crumpled horn in the spurs of many-folded, wooded Ida.
sentences.n: Poseidon turns to Apollo. εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς is the stock ‘the cattle of rolling gait and crumpled horn’. βουκολέεσκες is an iterative imperfect of βουκολέω ‘herd cattle’, the -εσκ- meaning ‘used to’. κνημοῖσι is the dative plural of κνημός, a spur or shoulder of a mountain. πολυπτύχου ‘many-folded’ and ὑληέσσης ‘wooded’ both agree with Ἴδης.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ μισθοῖο τέλος πολυγηθέες ὧραι
ἐξέφερον, τότε νῶϊ βιήσατο μισθὸν ἅπαντα
Λαομέδων ἔκπαγλος, ἀπειλήσας δ’ ἀπέπεμπε.
sentences.l:
But when at last the end of the wage the much-gladdening seasons
were bringing out, then he used force upon us two, as to the wage, all of it,
Laomedon, terrifying, and having threatened, was sending us away.
sentences.i: But when at last the seasons, bringers of much gladness, brought round the end of the wage, then terrifying Laomedon used force on us two and kept back all our wage, and sent us away with threats.
sentences.n: μισθοῖο τέλος is the end of the term for which they were hired, and the seasons ἐξέφερον ‘were bringing it out’. βιήσατο is the aorist middle of βιάομαι ‘use force’, here with two accusatives, νῶϊ ‘us two’ and μισθὸν ἅπαντα ‘the whole wage’: he kept it back by force. ἔκπαγλος ‘terrifying’ is a stock epithet. ἀπειλήσας ‘having threatened’; ἀπέπεμπε is the imperfect of ἀποπέμπω.

sentences.t:
σὺν μὲν ὅ γ’ ἠπείλησε πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθε
δήσειν, καὶ περάαν νήσων ἔπι τηλεδαπάων·
sentences.l:
Together, he for his part, threatened feet and hands, above,
to bind, and to carry across to far-off islands;
sentences.i: For his part he threatened to bind our feet and hands together, above, and to carry us across to far-off islands;
sentences.n: ὅ γε is Laomedon. σὺν … δήσειν is split (tmesis) for ‘to bind together’, and ὕπερθε is ‘above’; what lies above what is not clear, and the translation keeps the word. περάαν is περᾶν ‘to carry across’, that is to sell abroad. νήσων ἔπι τηλεδαπάων is ‘to far-off islands’ (ἔπι after its noun).

sentences.t: στεῦτο δ’ ὅ γ’ ἀμφοτέρων ἀπολεψέμεν οὔατα χαλκῷ.
sentences.l: And he declared, he for his part, to strip off the ears of both with bronze.
sentences.i: and he claimed that he would strip off the ears of both of us with bronze.
sentences.n: στεῦτο is ‘he declared, claimed’ (στεῦμαι ‘declare, claim’), followed by the future infinitive ἀπολεψέμεν ‘to strip off’ (ἀπολέπω ‘peel off’, here ‘cut off’). ἀμφοτέρων is ‘of both’, and χαλκῷ ‘with bronze’.

sentences.t:
νῶϊ δὲ ἄψορροι κίομεν κεκοτηότι θυμῷ
μισθοῦ χωόμενοι, τὸν ὑποστὰς οὐκ ἐτέλεσσε.
sentences.l:
But we two went, returning, with a resentful heart,
incensed about the wage, which, having promised it, he did not pay.
sentences.i: But we two went back with resentful hearts, incensed about the wage, which he had promised and did not pay.
sentences.n: νῶϊ δέ ‘but we two’ is a dual. ἄψορροι ‘returning’ and κίομεν ‘we went’ (from κίω, without augment). κεκοτηότι is the perfect participle of κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’, so ‘resentful’. μισθοῦ is a genitive of cause with χωόμενοι ‘incensed’. τόν is a relative ‘which’; ὑποστάς ‘having promised’; ἐτέλεσσε ‘paid’, with doubled σ.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δὴ νῦν λαοῖσι φέρεις χάριν, οὐδὲ μεθ’ ἡμέων
πειρᾷ ὥς κε Τρῶες ὑπερφίαλοι ἀπόλωνται
πρόχνυ κακῶς σὺν παισὶ καὶ αἰδοίῃς ἀλόχοισι.
sentences.l:
On his account, then, now to his people you bring favour, and not with us
make trial how the Trojans, overweening, may perish
forward on the knee, evilly, with their children and revered wives.”
sentences.i: And it is on his account that you now bring favour to his people, and do not try with us how the overweening Trojans may perish, utterly and in evil plight, with their children and their revered wives.”
sentences.n: τοῦ δή ‘on his account’ looks back to Laomedon, but the construction is loose. φέρεις χάριν is ‘you bring favour’. πειρᾷ is the second person of πειράομαι ‘make trial’, and ὥς κε … ἀπόλωνται ‘how they might perish’. πρόχνυ, from πρό + γόνυ ‘knee’, is ‘forward on the knee’, and so ‘utterly’; κακῶς ‘evilly’. αἰδοίῃς ‘revered’ goes with ἀλόχοισι ‘wives’. The edition prints no stop at the end of this line.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed lord far-working Apollo:
sentences.i: Then lord Apollo, who works from afar, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A paragraph begins, and Apollo answers Poseidon. τὸν δ’ αὖτε is ‘him then in turn’. ἄναξ ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων is ‘lord far-working Apollo’; whether ἑκάεργος means ‘far-working’ or ‘far-shooting’ is disputed.

sentences.t:
ἐννοσίγαι’ οὐκ ἄν με σαόφρονα μυθήσαιο
ἔμμεναι, εἰ δὴ σοί γε βροτῶν ἕνεκα πτολεμίξω
δειλῶν,
sentences.l:
“Earth-shaker, not would you call me sound-minded
to be, if indeed with you for the sake of mortals I should fight,
miserable ones,
sentences.i: “Earth-shaker, you would not call me sound-minded if I were to fight you for the sake of mortals, miserable ones,
sentences.n: ἐννοσίγαι’ is the vocative of ἐννοσίγαιος ‘earth-shaker’, another name for Poseidon. οὐκ ἄν … μυθήσαιο is ‘you would not call’ (optative of μυθέομαι), with με σαόφρονα ἔμμεναι ‘me to be sound-minded’. εἰ … πτολεμίξω is ‘if I should fight’, with σοί ‘with you’ and βροτῶν ἕνεκα ‘for the sake of mortals’. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence is long.

sentences.t:
οἳ φύλλοισιν ἐοικότες ἄλλοτε μέν τε
ζαφλεγέες τελέθουσιν ἀρούρης καρπὸν ἔδοντες,
ἄλλοτε δὲ φθινύθουσιν ἀκήριοι.
sentences.l:
who, like leaves, at one time
are very-blazing, eating the fruit of the plough-land,
and at another waste away, spiritless.
sentences.i: who, like leaves, at one time blaze with life, eating the fruit of the plough-land, and at another waste away, spiritless.
sentences.n: φύλλοισιν ἐοικότες is ‘like leaves’. ἄλλοτε μέν τε … ἄλλοτε δέ is ‘at one time … at another’. ζαφλεγέες, from ζα- ‘very’ and φλέγω ‘blaze’, means glowing with life. ἀρούρης καρπὸν ἔδοντες is ‘eating the fruit of the plough-land’, φθινύθουσιν ‘waste away’. ἀκήριοι ‘spiritless’ is from ἀ- and κῆρ ‘heart’; the formation is not certain. Men, Apollo says, are like leaves: brief and frail.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τάχιστα
παυώμεσθα μάχης·
sentences.l:
But very quickly
let us cease from battle;
sentences.i: But let us quickly cease from battle;
sentences.n: παυώμεσθα is a subjunctive with the epic ending -μεσθα, ‘let us cease’ (Attic παυώμεθα), taking the genitive μάχης ‘from battle’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ αὐτοὶ δηριαάσθων.
sentences.l: and let those men themselves fight on.”
sentences.i: and let them go on fighting by themselves.”
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ αὐτοί is ‘but they themselves’, the mortals. δηριαάσθων is the third-person plural imperative of δηριάομαι ‘fight on, contend’, in the uncontracted epic form. The speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας πάλιν ἐτράπετ’·
sentences.l: So then having spoken, back he turned;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and turned away;
sentences.n: A paragraph begins, and Apollo has finished speaking. ἐτράπετ’ is the aorist middle of τρέπω, ἐτράπετο ‘he turned’, and πάλιν ‘back’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
αἴδετο γάρ ῥα
πατροκασιγνήτοιο μιγήμεναι ἐν παλάμῃσι.
sentences.l:
for he was ashamed
to be mingled in the hands of his father’s brother.
sentences.i: for he was ashamed to meet his father’s brother hand to hand.
sentences.n: αἴδετο is the imperfect of αἴδομαι ‘feel shame before’. πατροκασιγνήτοιο is ‘of the father’s brother’: Poseidon was brother to Zeus, Apollo’s father. μιγήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of μίγνυμι ‘mingle’, and ἐν παλάμῃσι ‘in the hands’ gives ‘hand to hand’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ κασιγνήτη μάλα νείκεσε πότνια θηρῶν
Ἄρτεμις ἀγροτέρη, καὶ ὀνείδειον φάτο μῦθον·
sentences.l:
But him his sister greatly reviled, the lady of wild beasts,
Artemis of the wild, and a reproachful word she spoke:
sentences.i: But his sister, the lady of wild beasts, Artemis of the wild, reviled him sharply, and spoke a reproachful word:
sentences.n: κασιγνήτη ‘sister’ is Artemis, named in the next line. πότνια θηρῶν ‘lady of wild beasts’ is her stock title, and ἀγροτέρη ‘of the wild’ (from ἀγρός ‘country’) a second epithet. νείκεσε is ‘reviled’, ὀνείδειον ‘reproachful’, and φάτο the aorist middle of φημί.

sentences.t:
φεύγεις δὴ ἑκάεργε, Ποσειδάωνι δὲ νίκην
πᾶσαν ἐπέτρεψας, μέλεον δέ οἱ εὖχος ἔδωκας·
sentences.l:
“You flee, then, far-working one, and to Poseidon the victory
all you have entrusted, and an idle boast to him you have given;
sentences.i: “So you flee, you who work from afar, and have entrusted the whole victory to Poseidon, and given him an idle triumph;
sentences.n: Artemis speaks to Apollo. φεύγεις ‘you flee’ is a taunt, and ἑκάεργε is the vocative of ἑκάεργος ‘far-working’. ἐπέτρεψας is the aorist of ἐπιτρέπω ‘entrust’. μέλεον … εὖχος is ‘an idle boast’: she says he has handed Poseidon the right to boast.

sentences.t: νηπύτιε τί νυ τόξον ἔχεις ἀνεμώλιον αὔτως;
sentences.l: Childish one, why then do you have the bow, an empty thing, just so?
sentences.i: You child, why do you carry a bow, an empty thing, to no purpose?
sentences.n: νηπύτιε is again ‘childish one’. ἀνεμώλιον ‘empty’ comes from ἄνεμος ‘wind’, and αὔτως is ‘just so’, idly and to no purpose. The question mark is the Greek one, a semicolon.

sentences.t:
μή σευ νῦν ἔτι πατρὸς ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἀκούσω
εὐχομένου, ὡς τὸ πρὶν ἐν ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν,
ἄντα Ποσειδάωνος ἐναντίβιον πολεμίζειν.
sentences.l:
Let me not hear you, now any longer, in your father’s halls
declaring, as before among the immortal gods,
opposite Poseidon head-on to fight.”
sentences.i: Let me not hear you any more in your father’s halls declaring, as you did before among the immortal gods, that you will fight Poseidon head-on.”
sentences.n: μή σευ … ἀκούσω is ‘let me not hear you’, an aorist subjunctive after μή, with σευ (= σοῦ) in the genitive and the participle εὐχομένου ‘declaring’. ὡς τὸ πρὶν is ‘as before’. πατρός is Zeus. ἄντα Ποσειδάωνος is ‘opposite Poseidon’, and ἐναντίβιον ‘head-on’ (literally ‘with opposed force’) goes with πολεμίζειν.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τὴν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων,
ἀλλὰ χολωσαμένη Διὸς αἰδοίη παράκοιτις
νείκεσεν ἰοχέαιραν ὀνειδείοις ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and her not at all addressed far-working Apollo,
but, angered, the revered consort of Zeus
reviled the arrow-pourer with reproachful words:
sentences.i: So she spoke, but Apollo, who works from afar, made her no answer; and Zeus’ revered wife, in anger, reviled the one who showers her arrows, with reproachful words:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη is ‘to her he said nothing at all’. The next speaker is Hera: Διὸς αἰδοίη παράκοιτις is ‘the revered consort of Zeus’ (παράκοιτις is literally ‘one who lies beside’). χολωσαμένη ‘angered’. ἰοχέαιραν is Artemis; the second element of the word is disputed (χέω ‘pour’ or χαίρω ‘delight’).

sentences.t:
πῶς δὲ σὺ νῦν μέμονας κύον ἀδεὲς ἀντί’ ἐμεῖο
στήσεσθαι;
sentences.l:
“But how do you now purpose, dog, fearless one, opposite me
to take your stand?
sentences.i: “How do you now mean to take your stand against me, you dog, you fearless one?
sentences.n: Hera speaks. μέμονας is the perfect (with present sense) of μάω ‘be eager, resolve’, with the infinitive στήσεσθαι ‘to take a stand’. κύον ἀδεές is ‘dog, fearless one’; ἀδεές may be the vocative or an adverb ‘fearlessly’. ἀντί’ ἐμεῖο is ‘opposite me’ (ἀντία with the genitive).

sentences.t:
χαλεπή τοι ἐγὼ μένος ἀντιφέρεσθαι
τοξοφόρῳ περ ἐούσῃ, ἐπεὶ σὲ λέοντα γυναιξὶ
Ζεὺς θῆκεν, καὶ ἔδωκε κατακτάμεν ἥν κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα.
sentences.l:
Hard for you am I, in might, to oppose,
bow-bearing though you are, since a lion to women
Zeus made you, and gave you to kill whom you wish.
sentences.i: I am hard for you to stand against in might, bow-bearer though you are, since Zeus made you a lion to women and gave you leave to kill any you wish.
sentences.n: χαλεπή τοι ἐγώ is ‘I am hard for you’ (τοι = σοι), with ἀντιφέρεσθαι ‘to oppose, stand against’ and μένος an accusative of respect. τοξοφόρῳ περ ἐούσῃ is ‘though you are a bow-bearer’. ‘A lion to women’ points to the old belief that Artemis’ arrows bring women a swift death. κατακτάμεν is κατακτάμεναι ‘to kill’; ἥν κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is ‘whomever you wish’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι βέλτερόν ἐστι κατ’ οὔρεα θῆρας ἐναίρειν
ἀγροτέρας τ’ ἐλάφους ἢ κρείσσοσιν ἶφι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
It is, indeed, better, among the mountains, wild beasts to slay,
and wild deer, than with the stronger ones with force to fight.
sentences.i: It is better to slay wild beasts in the mountains, and wild deer, than to fight powerfully against those who are stronger.
sentences.n: ἤτοι … ἢ is ‘it is indeed better … than’. κατ’ οὔρεα is ‘in the mountains’ (οὔρεα is epic for ὄρη), and ἐναίρειν ‘to slay’. ἀγροτέρας ‘wild’ goes with ἐλάφους ‘deer’. κρείσσοσιν is ‘stronger ones’ and ἶφι ‘with force’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις πολέμοιο δαήμεναι, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῇς
ὅσσον φερτέρη εἴμ’, ὅτι μοι μένος ἀντιφερίζεις.
sentences.l:
But if you wish to learn of war, so that well you may know
how much stronger I am, since against me in might you set yourself.”
sentences.i: But if you want to learn about war, so that you may know well how much stronger I am, since you set yourself against me in might.”
sentences.n: δαήμεναι is the aorist infinitive ‘to learn’, with the genitive πολέμοιο. ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῇς is ‘so that you may know well’ (subjunctive of οἶδα). ὅσσον φερτέρη εἴμ’ is ‘how much stronger I am’, and ὅτι μοι μένος ἀντιφερίζεις ‘since you set yourself against me in might’. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἀμφοτέρας ἐπὶ καρπῷ χεῖρας ἔμαρπτε
σκαιῇ, δεξιτερῇ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀπ’ ὤμων αἴνυτο τόξα,
αὐτοῖσιν δ’ ἄρ’ ἔθεινε παρ’ οὔατα μειδιόωσα
ἐντροπαλιζομένην·
sentences.l:
She spoke, and both hands at the wrist she seized
with her left, and with her right from the shoulders took the bow,
and with the very things she beat about the ears, smiling,
her, turning back again and again;
sentences.i: So she said, and with her left hand seized both of Artemis’ hands at the wrist, and with her right took the bow from her shoulders, and smiling beat her about the ears with the bow itself as she kept turning back again and again;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα, καί is ‘she spoke, and’ (ἦ is the old ‘she said’); Hera is the subject throughout. σκαιῇ ‘left’ and δεξιτερῇ ‘right’ are datives of means with ‘hand’ understood. τόξα is the plural for the bow with its gear. αὐτοῖσιν ‘with the very things’; ἔθεινε is the imperfect of θείνω ‘strike’. ἐντροπαλιζομένην ‘turning back again and again’ is accusative, agreeing with Artemis, who is the unstated object.

sentences.t: ταχέες δ’ ἔκπιπτον ὀϊστοί.
sentences.l: and swift were falling out the arrows.
sentences.i: and the swift arrows fell out.
sentences.n: ἔκπιπτον is the imperfect of ἐκπίπτω ‘fall out’; the quiver is understood. ταχέες is ‘swift’, and ὀϊστοί ‘arrows’ is printed with the diaeresis. The arrows are the ones in her quiver.

sentences.t:
δακρυόεσσα δ’ ὕπαιθα θεὰ φύγεν ὥς τε πέλεια,
ἥ ῥά θ’ ὑπ’ ἴρηκος κοίλην εἰσέπτατο πέτρην
χηραμόν·
sentences.i: Tearful, the goddess fled away, like a dove which flew from a hawk into a hollow rock, into a cleft;
sentences.n: δακρυόεσσα is ‘tearful’, and ὕπαιθα ‘from under, away’. φύγεν is the unaugmented aorist of φεύγω. ὥς τε πέλεια begins a simile: the dove ὑπ’ ἴρηκος ‘from under a hawk’ (ἴρηξ = ἱέραξ) ‘flew into’ (εἰσέπτατο, aorist of εἰσπέτομαι) a hollow rock. χηραμόν ‘cleft’ stands in apposition.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ ἄρα τῇ γε ἁλώμεναι αἴσιμον ἦεν·
sentences.l: nor was it fated for her to be caught;
sentences.i: for it was not her fate to be caught;
sentences.n: τῇ is the dove. ἁλώμεναι is ἁλῶναι, the aorist infinitive of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be caught’ (passive in sense), and αἴσιμον ‘fated’. ἦεν is ἦν. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ὣς ἣ δακρυόεσσα φύγεν, λίπε δ’ αὐτόθι τόξα.
sentences.l: So she, tearful, fled, and left on the very spot the bow.
sentences.i: So she fled in tears, and left her bow there on the spot.
sentences.n: ὣς ἣ closes the simile: ‘so she’. αὐτόθι is ‘there on the spot’, and λίπε the unaugmented aorist of λείπω. τόξα is the plural of the bow, as before.

sentences.t: Λητὼ δὲ προσέειπε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης·
sentences.l: And to Leto addressed the guide, Argeïphontes:
sentences.i: And the guide, the slayer of Argus, said to Leto:
sentences.n: διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης is Hermes. The meaning of διάκτορος is not known (‘the guide’ is the usual rendering); ἀργεϊφόντης is usually ‘slayer of Argus’, but that is disputed. Λητώ (accusative) is Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis; Hermes’ speech is to her.

sentences.t: Λητοῖ ἐγὼ δέ τοι οὔ τι μαχήσομαι·
sentences.l: “Leto, I, for my part, with you will not at all fight;
sentences.i: “Leto, I for my part will not fight you at all;
sentences.n: Hermes speaks. Λητοῖ is the vocative of Λητώ. τοι is ‘to you’ (= σοι), and οὔ τι ‘not at all’. μαχήσομαι is the future of μάχομαι ‘fight’. The speech is short and courteous, and the unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον δὲ
πληκτίζεσθ’ ἀλόχοισι Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο·
sentences.l:
for grievous it is
to exchange blows with the wives of Zeus, the cloud-gatherer;
sentences.i: for it is a grievous thing to exchange blows with the wives of Zeus who gathers the clouds;
sentences.n: ἀργαλέον is ‘grievous’, with the infinitive πληκτίζεσθ’ (= πληκτίζεσθαι) ‘to exchange blows’, from πλήσσω ‘strike’, and the dative ἀλόχοισι ‘with the wives’. Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο is the stock ‘Zeus, the cloud-gatherer’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλα πρόφρασσα μετ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν
εὔχεσθαι ἐμὲ νικῆσαι κρατερῆφι βίηφιν.
sentences.l:
but, very ready-minded, among the immortal gods
declare yourself to have prevailed over me by strong might.”
sentences.i: but go ahead, with a ready mind, and declare among the immortal gods that you defeated me by strong might.”
sentences.n: πρόφρασσα is the feminine of πρόφρων, ‘ready-minded’. εὔχεσθαι ‘declare’ is an infinitive used as an imperative, with ἐμὲ νικῆσαι ‘that you defeated me’. κρατερῆφι βίηφιν has the old ending -φι twice, ‘by strong might’. The speech ends.
